claims.text: Sea snails crawl on their foot: its muscles contract in waves that run along it and deform a thin layer of mucus beneath. The mucus lowers friction and seals the gaps under the foot, so it grips and slides at once.
claims.evidenceNote: Describes land and sea snails generally; not measured for the species shown.

claims.text: Once a veliger has settled and metamorphosed, the young snail moves about on the seabed with its foot.

In the related cowrie Mauritia arabica, larvae ready to settle swam less and spread their velum less often, then spent more time on the bottom. They began crawling about 60 days after hatching and metamorphosed, losing the velum, at about 70 days.
claims.evidenceNote: Laboratory observations; in the same study tiger cowrie larvae did not settle, so this comes from a different cowrie.

claims.text: Young queen conch usually stay buried in the sediment for their first year of life.
claims.evidenceNote: Tertiary source summarising the species' life cycle.

claims.text: Queen conch do not crawl slowly along leaving slime trails. They hop: the foot pushes against the bottom and propels the shell up and forward. A study tracked 42 adults with loggers that record when each one is hopping or staying still.
claims.evidenceNote: From a press release on a peer-reviewed study and an encyclopedia account; the paper itself was not read.

claims.text: A nautilus squirts water through its funnel (hyponome) to thrust itself backwards and to make turns. It can swim head first or shell first; the faster it goes, the more efficient shell-first swimming becomes.
claims.evidenceNote: Government species profile and a laboratory study of swimming nautiluses.

claims.text: Nautiluses tracked at Osprey Reef in the Coral Sea spent the day resting at about 200 m or foraging below about 490 m, and the night moving continually between about 100 m and more than 700 m.
claims.evidenceNote: One tracked population; the study notes that nautiluses at Palau were deeper by day.

claims.text: Unlike the adult, a gastropod veliger has two ciliated, semicircular lobes resembling fins or wings, together called the velum, its main means of propulsion and of collecting food particles. The planktonic larval stage can carry it far from the adults that produced it; the velum and foot can be pulled into the shell to protect them, and the velum is lost at metamorphosis.
claims.evidenceNote: General description of gastropod veligers; the shape and size drawn here are illustrative, not of a particular species.

claims.text: Veligers have a band of long compound cilia in front of the mouth (the prototroch), a band of shorter cilia behind it (the metatroch), and a food groove between them whose cilia beat toward the mouth. The long cilia drive the water current; particles are caught between the two opposed bands and passed along the food groove to the mouth.
claims.evidenceNote: A peer-reviewed review of ciliary feeding; it also notes that how exactly particles are caught (the 'catch-up' idea, filmed in veligers by Strathmann & Leise, 1979) is a hypothesis.

claims.text: Tropical cowries produce many swimming veliger larvae from each egg capsule. In tiger cowries kept in the lab, a capsule held about 740 larvae on average, and a brood hatched over 1 to 3 days, with 90% of the larvae released overnight on the final day.
claims.evidenceNote: Counts and hatching timing are from captive tiger cowries (table 1 and section 3.1.1); 'numerous planktotrophic veligers per capsule' is stated for tropical cowries in general. How closely siblings stay together once in the open sea is not measured.

claims.text: In the wild, a brooding tiger cowrie was found in a crevice among coral rubble, sitting on its purplish-red egg mass. In the lab the capsules were glued in up to five layers to a hard surface and kept covered by the mother's foot until they hatched.
claims.evidenceNote: The field record is a single sighting on an intertidal reef in Singapore; the layering and covering foot are from captive brooders.

claims.text: Most cowries brood their eggs: the female glues her egg capsules to a hard surface and covers the egg mass with her foot until the larvae hatch.
claims.evidenceNote: Stated for cowries in general in the study's introduction; not observed for the money cowrie itself.

claims.text: Cone snails glue each egg capsule by an adhesive base to a hard surface, usually the underside of a rock or dead coral. In Hawaii, clusters held 1 to 68 capsules, each with 80 to about 10,000 eggs, and females were often found under the same rock.
claims.evidenceNote: Field collections of nine Hawaiian Conus species; Conus textile was not among them.

claims.text: Queen conch generally lay their egg masses in clean coral sand with little organic matter. The mass is one long tube folded and stuck into a compact clump, and sand grains stuck to it camouflage it.
claims.evidenceNote: A NOAA review summarising field studies (Randall 1964; D'Asaro 1965).

claims.text: Nautilus eggs have never been seen in the wild. In aquariums the female lays them in crevices or between corals, and they hatch after 9 to 15 months, depending on water temperature.
claims.evidenceNote: From captive breeding only; where wild nautilus lay their eggs is unknown.

claims.text: Newly hatched tiger cowrie veligers have translucent shells 200–242 micrometres long, tinged purple-red at the first whorl, a two-lobed velum, paired eyespots, a rudimentary foot and an operculum. Shells have not yet completed their first whorl. The velum expands into four distinctly bifurcated arms by 14 days after hatching.
claims.evidenceNote: Section 3.1.2 and microscopy figures 3–4, read directly. The money cowrie model borrows this general cowrie form, not a measured species-specific reconstruction. Displayed age progression is illustrative, not a calendar.
